# TypeScript — types checked before JavaScript executes

TypeScript type annotations do not automatically generate runtime validators. Understanding this distinction makes the following examples easier.

## 1. Structural typing

~~~ts
type User = { id: number };
const value = { id: 7, name: "Ada" };
const user: User = value;
console.log(user.id); // 7
~~~

Compatibility is based on the required object shape. Fresh object literals may also receive excess-property checks.

## 2. Discriminated unions

~~~ts
type Payment =
  | { kind: "cash" }
  | { kind: "card"; last4: string };
function describe(p: Payment): string {
  if (p.kind === "cash") return "cash";
  return p.last4; // narrowed to card
}
console.log(describe({ kind: "card", last4: "1234" }));
~~~

The common kind field distinguishes valid alternatives. The compiler knows that a card's last four digits exist only in the card branch.

## 3. Generics preserve a type relationship

~~~ts
function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
console.log(first([3, 7])); // 3
~~~

The output element type depends on the input element type T. Empty arrays yield undefined; the return type makes that possibility explicit.

## 4. Unknown input needs an actual runtime test

~~~ts
function asNumber(value: unknown): number | undefined {
  return typeof value === "number" ? value : undefined;
}
console.log(asNumber("7")); // undefined
~~~

A cast changes the compiler's interpretation; it cannot magically convert or validate untrusted JSON.

## 5. Async functions return Promises

~~~ts
async function double(): Promise<number> {
  return 21 * 2;
}
double().then(console.log); // 42
~~~

A Promise models eventual completion. It does not mean CPU work automatically runs on another thread.

**Official source:** [TypeScript Handbook](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html).
